text: A closure is a function that remembers values from the place where it was created, even after that place is gone.
make_multiplier takes a factor, and returns an inner function that multiplies by it.
The inner function closes over factor — it keeps a private reference to that value.
[chuckle] So times_three remembers three, and times_five remembers five, completely independently.
Calling times_three of ten gives thirty, while times_five of ten gives fifty — each carries its own factor.
[sniff] Closures can even hold state that changes over time, like this counter.
The nonlocal keyword lets the inner function modify the count from the enclosing function, not just read it.
So each call to counter bumps the number up and remembers it for next time.
[groan] That's a closure giving you private, persistent state — the same idea that powers decorators under the hood.
In the next one we take on generators. Comment PYTHON if you want the cheat sheet.
